warmup.q: The links between accounts and the devices and phones they use sit in one table, account_identifier(account_id, identifier_id), with one row for each account and each device or phone it used. You want the accounts exactly two steps from A-3101, where one step is "shares a device or phone with". How many times does the query join account_identifier?
options: Once: the table already holds every link
Four times: each step goes from an account to its devices and phones, then back to the other accounts that use them
It can't be written in SQL
warmup.why: One step crosses the link table twice: from the account to its identifiers, then from each identifier to the other accounts that use it. Two steps is four joins of the same table, three steps is six, and "up to N steps" needs a recursive query. "One join per step" is the tempting answer, because we say "one step", but each step through a shared phone is two links. A graph store follows those links directly instead of joining.

sections.h: Every step through a shared phone costs a table two joins
sections.html:
Let's start with the question. The fraud team flagged account A-3101 at 09:12. They want every other account linked to it through a shared identifier, a device or phone number used to log in. Some are linked directly, and some through up to two more accounts in between. Accounts linked like that may be a ring, a group of people cheating together.

First, store the links in a table, the way the last lesson stored invitations. The table account_identifier(account_id, identifier_id) has one row per link: this account used this identifier. Each column has an index, a sorted list of the column's values with the place of each row, like the index at the back of a book.

One step, "accounts that share an identifier with A-3101", crosses the table twice. Look up A-3101's rows through the index on account_id to find its identifiers. Then, for each identifier, look up its other rows through the index on identifier_id. That's a self join, a join of a table with itself. Two steps is four joins, three steps is six, and "up to three" is the last lesson's recursive CTE. The query grows with every step you allow.

So does the work. An index is stored as a B+tree, a sorted tree of fixed-size blocks called pages, and a lookup reads one page per level, from the top down. For millions of rows that's 3 or 4 pages, usually already in memory, so a few microseconds. But every step multiplies the rows. Say each account has 3 identifiers and each identifier is shared by 2 accounts (made-up numbers, to see the shape): every step fans out by about 6. One step touches 6 rows, three steps about 6 x 6 x 6 = 216, six steps about 47,000. The planner, the part of the database that decides how to run a query, has to guess how many rows each join will make. Its guesses get worse with every join (the Storage engines track's lesson on query optimization shows why).

Now store the data the other way round. Think of a detective's pinboard: a photo for each account and each phone, with a string between each account and every phone it used. To take one step, put your finger on A-3101's photo, follow its strings to its phones, then follow each phone's strings to the other photos. You never search the board.

That's what a graph database stores. Neo4j is a database program built for graphs. In it, each node (a photo) has a record that leads to its relationships (the strings), and each relationship records the nodes at both ends. Following one is a pointer read: the record says where the next record is, and Neo4j goes straight there. Neo4j calls this index-free adjacency, because finding a node's neighbours needs no index. The cost of a step doesn't depend on how many accounts exist.

A graph store answers a question by walking: find a start node through an index, then follow relationships outward, and pay only for the part of the graph you touch. That's the picture for this lesson.

The fan-out doesn't go away. Both designs pay for every path they explore, and the Try it shows a walk that jumps from 2 paths to 14 at the third step. What changes is the price of each step, and how easily you can say "up to N steps". If your questions are one or two steps of a known shape, stay with tables. When they're paths of unknown length, rings or cycles, a graph store fits. Next, we'll learn to read and write the graph.

try.title: Start Neo4j and count what each step touches
steps: From the labs folder, start Neo4j 2026.10 Community, the free edition: docker compose -f env/neo4j.yml up -d --wait. (Docker runs small, separate Linux systems on your laptop.) It takes about 20 seconds on an idle laptop, longer on a busy one, and uses up to 1.5 GB of Docker's memory.

Load the fraud graph: docker compose -f env/neo4j.yml exec neo4j cypher-shell -f /sfz/nosql-11-fraud.cypher. cypher-shell is Neo4j's command-line window. The file deletes whatever is in the database, then creates 13 accounts, 15 devices and phones, and the links between them.

Open a prompt with docker compose -f env/neo4j.yml exec neo4j cypher-shell and paste the two queries below. They're written in Cypher, which the next section explains; for now, read each arrow as a string on the pinboard. Before the second query, predict how many paths and accounts each step adds. aside.title: If following a pointer is so cheap, why doesn't every database store links this way?
aside.html: Because pointers make one kind of question cheap and others dearer. A table keeps its rows packed together, which suits adding up a whole column, finding rows by any value, and changing many rows in one go. A graph store spreads its records out by link: every new relationship has to be linked into the relationship lists of both its nodes, and a total over all payments reads records scattered across the file. Tables work links out at query time, which suits most questions well enough. It's a trade, and the last section shows where the graph loses.

sections.h: Nodes, relationships and properties, and a query you draw
sections.html:
The pinboard has two kinds of thing on it, and so does a graph database. A node is a thing: an account, a device, a phone number. It has one or more labels, which say what kind of thing it is (:Account, :Device), and properties, named values such as id: 'A-3101' or flagged: true. A relationship is a string between exactly two nodes. It has one type, such as USES or TRANSFERRED_TO, a direction, and properties of its own, such as amountMinor: 95000 on a transfer (amounts are in cents, so that's 950.00). If you think in tables, a node is a row, and a relationship is a row of a link table, except that it's stored as a link instead of being worked out by a join.

This shape is called a property graph. It's a data model, a way of shaping data, not one product. The same model fits in two tables, vertices(id, label, properties) and edges(id, tail_id, head_id, label, properties), with an index on each end; that's what the last lesson's CREATE PROPERTY GRAPH declares over ordinary tables. Neo4j and Memgraph, another graph database, store it natively, in files of their own. Amazon Neptune, Amazon's cloud graph database, serves it with openCypher and Gremlin, two other graph languages. Apache AGE adds it to PostgreSQL, the free database program of the last lesson, and two commercial databases, Oracle and Google's Spanner, map it onto tables.

Two facts hold in all of them. A relationship joins exactly two nodes. So a fact about three things, such as a card used at a shop through one card reader, needs a node of its own for the payment. And a new kind of node needs no migration, the careful change to a table's columns from "SQL from the JVM: JDBC, pools, batching and migrations". Add :Card nodes tomorrow, and every old query still runs.

Cypher, Neo4j's query language, lets you draw the shape you're looking for in plain text. Round brackets are nodes, arrows are relationships, and square brackets hold a relationship's details:

MATCH (a:Account {id: 'A-1001'})-[:USES]->(x)
RETURN labels(x)[0] AS kind, x.id AS id

MATCH finds every place in the graph where the drawing fits, and gives the names in it (a, x) to what it found. WHERE filters the matches, and RETURN says what to send back. Aggregates such as count(*), which count or add up, group by the other returned columns, with no GROUP BY. Direction matters: (a)<-[:TRANSFERRED_TO]-(sender) finds who paid a, and an arrow with no head matches either way. CREATE writes a pattern. MERGE finds a pattern, or creates it when it's missing, which is how you load events that may arrive twice.

Neo4j moved to version numbers that are dates in January 2025: 2026.10.0 came out on 20 October 2026, and this lesson runs 2026.10.1. Version 5.26 is the long-term-support line, the one that keeps getting fixes for years. The query language has versions of its own. Cypher 5 has been frozen since 2025.06, new features go into Cypher 25, and Cypher 25 is the default since 2026.02. The PROFILE output later in this lesson says so.

There's a standard now, too. GQL (ISO/IEC 39075:2024) was published on 12 April 2024, the first new database language from ISO, the international standards body, since SQL. Its pattern matching grew out of Cypher, and Neo4j documents that Cypher 25 covers most of GQL's required features, with a list of gaps and small differences. So GQL hasn't replaced Cypher; Cypher is moving toward it. Spanner Graph and Microsoft Fabric, Microsoft's cloud data platform, implement GQL too, and a MATCH ... RETURN like the one above reads the same in both.

One step at a time works, but the ring question repeats the same step. Next, we'll write the repeat.

sections.h: Repeating a step: the ring, and money that comes back
sections.html:
The ring question repeats one step: account, identifier, account. Cypher 25 writes a repeated piece of a pattern as a quantified path pattern: the piece in brackets, followed by how many times it may repeat.

MATCH (start:Account {id: 'A-3101'})
      ((:Account)-[:USES]->(x)<-[:USES]-(:Account)){1,3}
      (other:Account)
WHERE other <> start
RETURN other.id AS account, min(size(x)) AS steps

{1,3} means one to three repeats. The start node fills the first (:Account) of the first repeat, and other is the last account of the last one. A name used inside the brackets, x, becomes a list with one entry per repeat. So size(x), the length of that list, is the number of steps, and min(size(x)) is the fewest steps to each account. The stepper walks this query one step at a time.

When the repeated piece is a single relationship, you can put the count on the relationship alone. Money that comes back to where it started is a path of 3 to 6 transfers that ends at its first node:

MATCH p = (a:Account)-[:TRANSFERRED_TO]->{3,6}(a)
RETURN [n IN nodes(p) | n.id] AS cycle

nodes(p) lists the nodes along the path p, and [n IN nodes(p) | n.id] turns that into a list of their ids. Older code and blog posts write the repeat as -[:TRANSFERRED_TO*3..6]->. It still works, but Neo4j's manual says it doesn't follow GQL, and unlike a quantified path pattern, it can't hold a WHERE inside the repeated part.

Two rules decide what comes back. Within one match, Cypher never uses the same relationship twice, so a path can't run back and forth along one string forever. And a cycle, a path that comes back to its start, has no natural first node. The ring A-3101, A-3103, A-3104 is found once starting from each of its three accounts. The Try it counts the copies, and the lab keeps one by asking that the start has the smallest id in the cycle.

The lower bound matters too. Two friends who pay each other back make a cycle of 2, which {3,6} leaves out on purpose.

The ring walk also found four ordinary customers at step 3. Next, we'll see why, and what makes a walk start fast.

steps: In the same cypher-shell, run the two queries below.

sections.h: Where a walk starts, and the busy node that floods it
sections.html:
Every walk starts somewhere, and the start is the one place a graph needs an index. Without one, MATCH (f:Account {id: 'A-3101'}) reads every Account node and checks its id. The plan shows NodeByLabelScan, then Filter. On 13 accounts that's 14 database hits, Neo4j's count of the records it read. On 10 million accounts it's 10 million, before the first step. A uniqueness constraint, a rule that no two accounts share an id, also builds an index. Then the plan starts with NodeUniqueIndexSeek instead: 2 hits, whatever the size. The Expand(All) steps after it are the walk itself, and they don't change. PROFILE runs a query and shows this plan, with the rows and hits of every step, like EXPLAIN ANALYZE in PostgreSQL.

On the pinboard, the index is the list by the door that says where each photo is pinned. You use it once, to find the first photo, and then you follow strings.

The second thing to watch is the node everyone touches. The store kiosk in the lab's graph has 5 accounts. A real kiosk, a shared office Wi-Fi network or a test card that a payment company hands out can link 50,000 accounts. Every walk through it brings all of them in. That's a supernode, the train station on the pinboard with strings to half the city. Here the pinboard picture breaks. On a real board you see every string at once, while the database only sees the strings your walk follows. A walk with no limit can wander into far more of the graph than you meant.

There are three ways out. Filter the supernode out inside the pattern, by a property, as ring.cypher does with the kiosk. Cap its degree, the number of relationships it has, with WHERE COUNT { (x)<-[:USES]-() } < 50 on the identifier. Or don't store it: an identifier that thousands of people share proves nothing about cheating, so leave that relationship out.

A walk with no bounds will find the supernode. Bound every walk.

Know, too, when a graph is the wrong store. "Total payments per shop per day" visits every transfer and follows nothing. That's a job for a table and a GROUP BY, or for a column store, a database built for adding up columns. The ledger, the record of every movement of money, takes thousands of writes a second, and it belongs in the payments database, not a graph. In practice, the graph is a second copy, fed from the system of record, the store that holds the official version of each fact. The payments program writes to its database. Kafka, a program that keeps a log of messages and lets other programs read it, carries each event. A small program reads those events and MERGEs accounts, devices and transfers into Neo4j for the fraud team's walks. The worked example builds it.

The Storage engines track's lesson "Inside Neo4j: native graph storage, memory and clustering" goes underneath. It shows how Neo4j lays out nodes and relationships on disk so that a step is a pointer, how to size its memory, and how it runs on several machines. This lesson's graph had labels, properties and a language built for them. Next, we'll take a graph apart into its smallest pieces.

try.title: Find the supernode, then watch the start of the plan change
steps: In the same cypher-shell, run the block below. The first query ranks identifiers by how many accounts use them.
Compare the two PROFILE plans, reading each from the bottom up (the bottom step runs first). Which step changed, and how many database hits did it save?
Stop Neo4j when you're done: docker compose -f env/neo4j.yml down -v.

code.title: in cypher-shell
code.html: // which identifiers do the most accounts share? MATCH (x)<-[:USES]-(a:Account) RETURN labels(x)[0] AS kind, x.id AS id, count(a) AS accounts ORDER BY accounts DESC, id LIMIT 3; PROFILE MATCH (f:Account {id: 'A-3101'})-[:USES]->(x)<-[:USES]-(other:Account) RETURN other.id AS account, x.id AS via; CREATE CONSTRAINT account_id IF NOT EXISTS FOR (a:Account) REQUIRE a.id IS UNIQUE; PROFILE MATCH (f:Account {id: 'A-3101'})-[:USES]->(x)<-[:USES]-(other:Account) RETURN other.id AS account, x.id AS via;

refs.title: Neo4j Cypher Manual: MERGE (and why it needs a uniqueness constraint under concurrency)

opening:
Picture a payments company on a Monday morning. Overnight, one account made a run of odd payments, and the fraud team, the people who look for cheating, has flagged it as suspicious. Their question: which other accounts share a phone or laptop with this one, directly or through up to two other accounts? People who cheat together often share phones.

It's easy to think that a table with an index on every column answers this as fast as anything can. Each lookup takes microseconds. But every step through a shared phone is two lookups and a join, and the rows multiply at each step.

In Recursive CTEs: trees and graphs in SQL, we walked chains with a loop of joins. In this lesson, we'll keep the links in Neo4j, a database built for graphs, and draw our questions in its language, Cypher. We'll find a ring of accounts, and money that comes back where it started, and see what makes a walk start fast and what floods it. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a flagged account and a question about who else is involved. In tables, every step through a shared phone cost two lookups and a join. On the graph, it's two strings followed from a photo. The walk pays only for what it touches, until it reaches a kiosk everyone used.

Look at a social app you use. "People you may know" is often a walk of two steps: friends of your friends. Ask how many people that walk would reach if one friend knew ten thousand.

Next, we'll take a graph apart into facts of three parts, write rules that walk it for us, and meet GraphQL, which has "graph" in its name but isn't a database.

compare.title: The ring around A-3101, up to three steps, in SQL and in Cypher

a.label: PostgreSQL: recursive CTE
a.title: a link table account_identifier(account_id, identifier_id)
a.html: WITH RECURSIVE ring(account_id, steps, path) AS ( SELECT 'A-3101'::text, 0, ARRAY['A-3101'] UNION ALL SELECT b.account_id, r.steps + 1, r.path || b.account_id FROM ring r JOIN account_identifier a ON a.account_id = r.account_id -- my identifiers JOIN account_identifier b ON b.identifier_id = a.identifier_id -- their other users AND b.account_id <> ALL (r.path) -- never walk back WHERE r.steps < 3 ) SELECT account_id, min(steps) AS steps FROM ring WHERE steps > 0 GROUP BY account_id ORDER BY steps, account_id;

b.label: Neo4j: quantified path pattern
b.title: Cypher 25
b.html: MATCH (start:Account {id: 'A-3101'}) ((:Account)-[:USES]->(x)<-[:USES]-(:Account)){1,3} (other:Account) WHERE other <> start RETURN other.id AS account, min(size(x)) AS steps ORDER BY steps, account;

compare.note: Both return the same eight accounts on the lab's graph (checked on PostgreSQL 18). The SQL spells out the walk: a starting row, a recursive step that joins the link table twice, a path array so it never walks back, and a step counter. Every step is two index lookups and a join, and the planner has to guess the size of a loop whose end it can't see. The Cypher draws one step and says how often it repeats. Neo4j follows stored relationships and never uses the same relationship twice in a path. Neither one stops a supernode from flooding the result: both need the kiosk filtered out by hand.

worked.title: Feed the fraud graph from Kafka without copies

steps.say: Start from the event. Each time someone logs in, the login program sends one message to Kafka, onto a topic (a named log of messages) called auth.logins. The message's key is the account. Kafka delivers each message at least once, so the program that reads them will sometimes see the same login twice.

First try: CREATE the account, the device and the link. A second delivery of the same message creates a second A-3101 node and a second relationship. Every walk then counts the copy, and the ring query reports A-3101 as its own neighbour.
steps.code: // wrong: every delivery adds new nodes and a new relationship CREATE (a:Account {id: $accountId})-[:USES]->(d:Device {id: $deviceId})

steps.say: Use MERGE, one piece at a time. Each MERGE finds the pattern if it exists and creates it if not. Merging the two nodes first, then the relationship between them, reuses an account that's already there instead of creating a whole new path. ON CREATE SET runs only the first time, and SET runs every time.
steps.code: MERGE (a:Account {id: $accountId}) MERGE (d:Device {id: $deviceId}) MERGE (a)-[u:USES]->(d) ON CREATE SET u.firstSeen = datetime($at) SET u.lastSeen = datetime($at)

steps.say: Add the constraints. Neo4j's manual is plain about this: when several programs write at once, MERGE alone promises that the pattern exists, not that there's only one. Two readers handling two parts of the topic can both create A-3101. A uniqueness constraint closes that gap, and it gives every MERGE an index seek instead of a scan of every account.
steps.code: CREATE CONSTRAINT account_id IF NOT EXISTS FOR (a:Account) REQUIRE a.id IS UNIQUE; CREATE CONSTRAINT device_id IF NOT EXISTS FOR (d:Device) REQUIRE d.id IS UNIQUE;

steps.say: Run it from the reading program with the Neo4j Java driver 6.3, the library a Java or Kotlin program uses to talk to Neo4j. executableQuery runs the statement in a transaction and retries it on temporary errors. The parameters, the names that start with $, keep the statement's text the same every time, so Neo4j plans it once. The program tells Kafka it's done (commitSync) only after the writes, so after a crash the messages come again, and MERGE absorbs the repeat.
steps.code: // a $$ string (Kotlin 2.2 and later): a single $ stays a literal $, which Cypher needs for parameters val merge = $$""" MERGE (a:Account {id: $accountId}) MERGE (d:Device {id: $deviceId}) MERGE (a)-[u:USES]->(d) ON CREATE SET u.firstSeen = datetime($at) SET u.lastSeen = datetime($at) """.trimIndent() for (record in consumer.poll(Duration.ofMillis(500))) { val login = parse(record.value()) // accountId, deviceId, at driver.executableQuery(merge) .withParameters(mapOf("accountId" to login.accountId, "deviceId" to login.deviceId, "at" to login.at)) .execute() } consumer.commitSync() // after the writes: a crash means a replay, and MERGE absorbs it

lab.title: Write the fraud team's four queries in Cypher, against a real Neo4j
steps: Make sure Docker is running, then run the tests from the labs folder. The first run starts one neo4j:2026.10.1 container through Testcontainers, a library that starts real databases in Docker for tests; that takes a minute or two. Before every test, the graph from the lesson is loaded again. One test passes (it only checks the seed data), and eight fail.

Each exercise is one .cypher file holding a placeholder query. The comment at the top gives the parameters, the columns and the order the tests expect. You can try a query in the lesson's cypher-shell first.
Write schema.cypher: one statement that creates a uniqueness constraint named account_id on Account.id. One more test passes.

Write suspicious-pairs.cypher and ring.cypher. The ring test runs your query with and without the kiosk, and a plan test checks that it starts with NodeUniqueIndexSeek once the constraint exists. Five more pass.
Write money-cycles.cypher, with each cycle once. All nine pass.
hints: A uniqueness constraint: CREATE CONSTRAINT account_id IF NOT EXISTS FOR (a:Account) REQUIRE a.id IS UNIQUE.

Pairs: match (a:Account)-[:USES]->(x)<-[:USES]-(b:Account) WHERE a.id < b.id, so each pair comes once. Then WITH a, b, x ORDER BY x.id before collect(x.id), so the list comes out sorted. (WITH passes rows on to the next part of the query.) Filter with WHERE size(shared) >= $minShared after the WITH.

Ring: put a filter on the identifier inside the repeated part: (x WHERE NOT coalesce(x.kind, '') IN $skipKinds). Phones have no kind, which is why coalesce, "the first value that isn't null", is there.

Cycles: -[:TRANSFERRED_TO]->{3,6} back to the same (a), and WHERE all(n IN nodes(p) WHERE a.id <= n.id) keeps the copy that starts at the smallest id. reduce(total = 0, t IN relationships(p) | total + t.amountMinor) adds up the amounts.
A ; at the end is fine; the tests strip it. Comments start with //.

drill.title: The ring query from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lesson and the lab. Write the Cypher that returns every account one to three steps from A-3101 (one step is account, shared device or phone, account), skipping identifiers whose kind is 'store kiosk', with the fewest steps to each. Then write one sentence on what makes the query start fast.

answer.html: MATCH (start:Account {id: 'A-3101'}) ((:Account)-[:USES]->(x WHERE coalesce(x.kind, '') <> 'store kiosk')<-[:USES]-(:Account)){1,3} (other:Account) WHERE other <> start RETURN other.id AS account, min(size(x)) AS steps // x holds one identifier per step ORDER BY steps, account; // Fast start: a uniqueness constraint on Account.id gives the planner an index, // so the walk begins with NodeUniqueIndexSeek instead of scanning every Account.

recap: In tables, one step through a shared phone is two index lookups in a link table and a join, and "up to N steps" is a recursive query that grows with every step. A graph store keeps each node's relationships with it, so a step is a pointer read.

A property graph is a data model, not a product: nodes with labels and properties, and relationships with one type, a direction and properties. Neo4j and Memgraph store it natively, and SQL/PGQ lays it over tables. Cypher matches a pattern drawn in text: (a:Account)-[:USES]->(x).

Quantified path patterns repeat a piece of a pattern, ((...)-[:USES]->(x)<-[:USES]-(...)){1,3}, and -[:TRANSFERRED_TO]->{3,6} repeats one relationship. The older *3..6 still works but doesn't follow GQL. A cycle is found once from each of its nodes.
A walk starts from an index: a uniqueness constraint gives you one, and the plan starts with NodeUniqueIndexSeek instead of NodeByLabelScan.
Neo4j uses date-style versions (2026.10, with 5.26 for long-term support) and Cypher 25 by default. GQL, ISO/IEC 39075:2024, made Cypher's pattern style a standard, and Cypher is moving toward it.

The limit: a graph store makes each step cheap, not the whole walk. One supernode can flood any walk, so bound every walk, and use the graph for walks, rings and cycles, fed from the system of record, never as the ledger itself.

explain.prompt: A teammate says: "Our tables have an index on every column. A graph database can't follow links faster than an indexed join." Explain what each one does for every step, where the graph store really wins, and where it doesn't.
explain.answer: For each step, the table finds the next rows through an index: it reads down a B+tree, a few pages that are usually in memory, then joins. A step through a shared phone is two of those, one to find the account's phones and one to find the other accounts that use them. "Up to three steps" becomes a recursive query whose size the planner has to guess blind. A graph store keeps each node's relationships with the node, so a step is a pointer read whose cost doesn't depend on how many accounts exist, and the query is a pattern with a repeat count instead of a loop of joins. Both still pay for every path they explore: one shared kiosk can turn 3 accounts into 4,800 in either one, so you bound the walk and filter supernodes either way. The graph wins for walks of unknown length, rings and cycles, which is the fraud team's work. It loses for adding up whole tables and for being the ledger. Those stay in the payments database, and the graph is fed from it, through Kafka, with MERGE and uniqueness constraints so that repeated messages don't make copies.

deeper.html:
Cypher's default rule for a match is "different relationships": within one match, no relationship appears twice, but a node may. That's why a ring walk can come back through the start account by a different identifier, and why WHERE other <> start is needed. Cypher 25 lets you name the rule. MATCH DIFFERENT RELATIONSHIPS is the default (GQL calls it DIFFERENT EDGES), and MATCH REPEATABLE ELEMENTS lets a path reuse relationships. On the lab's graph, (a:Account {id: 'A-3101'})-[:USES]-{2}(b) finds 2 paths by default and 4 with repeatable elements: the extra two go out to a device and straight back. A walk that may repeat must have an upper bound, or it never ends.

For "how far apart are these two accounts", ask for the shortest path instead of listing every path: MATCH p = SHORTEST 1 (a:Account {id: 'A-3101'})(()-[:USES]-()){1,8}(b:Account {id: 'A-4003'}) RETURN length(p). On the lab's graph it returns 6 relationships, from A-3101 through D-77, A-3102, P-0199, A-3103 and the kiosk to A-4003. It stops at the shortest match instead of listing every route, which matters as soon as a supernode is in reach.

GQL and Cypher 25 still differ in small ways. Neo4j's list of gaps includes GQL's commands for sessions and transactions, and sum() over no rows gives null in GQL but 0 in Cypher.

Neo4j Community, the free edition this lesson runs, is one server on its own. Clustering is in the paid Enterprise edition: several primary servers that agree on every write through Raft, a method for machines to agree (the Consistency and consensus track builds it), plus secondaries that serve reads. Online backup is Enterprise only, too. For a fraud graph that's rebuilt from Kafka, one server plus a topic you can replay is a fair design: losing the server costs a rebuild, not data.

Graph algorithms are a separate tool from pattern matching. Neo4j's Graph Data Science library works out things like PageRank (how central each node is), community detection (which accounts form tight groups) and node similarity over the whole graph, in memory. Fraud teams often run community detection every night, store each account's group as a property, and then match patterns within a group. Patterns tell you how two accounts are connected; the algorithms tell you which groups exist at all.

The last lesson showed the other road. SQL/PGQ puts the same pattern syntax inside SQL, through GRAPH_TABLE, and GQL and SQL/PGQ share one pattern language, so a MATCH clause reads alike in both. Oracle Database 23ai and later run SQL/PGQ over ordinary tables. Stonebraker and Pavlo argue that this road wins for most uses; Neo4j's answer is the pointer-per-step storage that the Storage engines track opens up.
